q: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
explain: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and about 11 times wider than Earth, with an equatorial diameter of about 142,984 km.
hook: Jupiter, king of the Roman gods, is king of the planets.

sources.title: Planet Sizes and Locations in Our Solar System - NASA Science
sources.quote: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. It’s about 11 times wider than Earth with an equatorial diameter of 88,846 miles (about 142,984 kilometers).

sources.title: About the Planets - NASA Science
sources.quote: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun, and the largest planet in our solar system.

q: Which planet is nearest to the Sun?
explain: Mercury is the smallest planet and the nearest to the Sun, and it is the fastest planet, orbiting the Sun every 88 Earth days.
hook: Mercury, the swift messenger god, runs the shortest lap around the Sun.

sources.title: Mercury: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and nearest to the Sun.

sources.title: About the Planets - NASA Science
sources.quote: Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun, and the smallest planet in our solar system.

q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
explain: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, making it hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

sources.title: Venus: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Its thick atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet in our solar system with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead — about 872 degrees Fahrenheit (467 Celsius).

sources.title: Temperatures Across Our Solar System - NASA Science
sources.quote: So Venus – not Mercury – is the hottest planet in our solar system.

q: On which planet is Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the solar system?
explain: Olympus Mons on Mars stands more than 25 miles (40 km) tall from base to summit, dwarfing Mount Everest.
hook: Mount Olympus was home of the gods; Olympus Mons is home on the Red Planet.

sources.title: Mars: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Mars is home to the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons .

sources.title: Olympus Mons | Description, Height, & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: Olympus Mons , volcano on the planet Mars , the highest point on the planet and the largest known volcano in the solar system .

q: Which planet rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle to its orbit, so it appears to spin on its side?
explain: Uranus is tilted about 97.77 degrees, which may be the result of a collision with an Earth-sized object long ago, and gives it the most extreme seasons in the solar system.
hook: Uranus rolls around the Sun like a ball.

sources.title: Uranus: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Uranus rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit. This unique tilt makes Uranus appear to spin sideways, orbiting the Sun like a rolling ball.

sources.title: Uranus - NASA Science
sources.quote: It rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit. This unique tilt makes Uranus appear to spin on its side.

q: On what date did Apollo 11 make the first crewed landing on the Moon?
explain: Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969 and landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, in the Sea of Tranquility.

sources.title: What Was the Apollo Program? - NASA
sources.quote: The first moon landing occurred on July 20, 1969, on the Apollo 11 mission.

sources.title: The Apollo Program (1963 - 1972) - NSSDCA
sources.quote: Apollo 11 Launched 16 July 1969 Landed on Moon 20 July 1969 Sea of Tranquility Returned to Earth 24 July 1969

sources.title: A Brief History of the Apollo Program | Smithsonian Institution
sources.quote: In LM Eagle July 20, Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin made the historic first landing on the moon. Their site was in the Sea of Tranquility.

q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
explain: On Apollo 11, Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

sources.title: A Brief History of the Apollo Program | Smithsonian Institution
sources.quote: Armstrong became the first human to walk on the moon, followed by Aldrin, and they brought home the first samples from another celestial body.

sources.title: How Many People Have Been to the Moon? | Britannica
sources.quote: He was followed quickly by the second person to walk on the Moon, Buzz Aldrin , while Michael Collins remained in the Command Module orbiting the Moon.

q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in lunar orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon?
explain: Michael Collins piloted the command module Columbia in lunar orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the lunar module Eagle.

sources.title: What Was the Apollo Program? - NASA
sources.quote: The crew of Apollo 11 was Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin. Armstong and Aldrin walked on the lunar surface while Collins remained in orbit around the moon.

sources.title: A Brief History of the Apollo Program | Smithsonian Institution
sources.quote: Michael Collins piloted the CSM Columbia mothership.

q: Which mission was the last Apollo lunar landing?
explain: Apollo 17 flew in December 1972; Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt landed in the Taurus-Littrow valley.

sources.title: Apollo 17 - NASA
sources.quote: The Apollo Program's last lunar landing mission, and the first to include an astronaut-scientist, landed in the Moon's Taurus-Littrow Valley.

sources.title: A Brief History of the Apollo Program | Smithsonian Institution
sources.quote: Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt made the sixth and last lunar landing by humans, piloting LM Challenger to the Taurus-Littrow site

q: How many astronauts have walked on the Moon?
explain: Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972; 24 astronauts in total traveled to the Moon during Apollo.
hook: Six landings times two moonwalkers each equals twelve.

sources.title: What Was the Apollo Program? - NASA
sources.quote: A total of 12 astronauts walked on the moon.

sources.title: How Many People Have Been to the Moon? | Britannica
sources.quote: In fact, during nine Apollo missions, 24 astronauts (all Americans) went to the Moon, and 12 of them walked on it.

q: Roughly how many kilometers are in one light-year?
explain: A light-year is a unit of distance, not time: the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year, about 9.46 trillion km (5.88 trillion miles).

sources.title: What is a light-year? - NASA Science
sources.quote: Light zips through interstellar space at 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second and 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers) per year.

sources.title: Light-year | Distance, Measurement, Time | Britannica
sources.quote: A light-year equals about 9.46073 × 10 12 km (5.87863 × 10 12 miles), or 63,241 astronomical units.

q: Approximately how long is one astronomical unit (AU), the average Earth-Sun distance?
explain: The AU is about 149.6 million km (93 million miles); in 2012 the IAU fixed it at exactly 149,597,870.7 km.

sources.title: Astronomical unit (AU, or au) | Britannica
sources.quote: An astronomical unit (AU) is a unit of length equal to the average distance between Earth and the Sun, which is about 149.6 million kilometers (92.96 million miles).

sources.title: Cosmic Distances - NASA Science
sources.quote: One AU is the distance from the Sun to Earth's orbit, which is about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers).

q: About how long does sunlight take to travel from the Sun to Earth?
explain: Earth is about eight light-minutes from the Sun, so we see the Sun as it was roughly 8 minutes ago.

sources.title: Cosmic Distances - NASA Science
sources.quote: Light years also provide some helpful perspective on solar system distances: the Sun is about 8 light minutes from Earth.

sources.title: Chapter 1: The Solar System - NASA Science
sources.quote: 8.3 minutes | 149,600,000 km | Sun to Earth (1 au)

q: Which star is the nearest to the Sun?
explain: Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf about 4.24 light-years away, is part of the Alpha Centauri triple star system.

sources.title: The Nearest Neighbor Star - Imagine the Universe! - NASA
sources.quote: Of the three stars in the system, the dimmest - called Proxima Centauri - is actually the nearest star to the Sun.

sources.title: Sun: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Its nearest stellar neighbor is the Alpha Centauri triple star system: red dwarf star Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light-years away, and Alpha Centauri A and B – two sunlike stars orbiting each other – are 4.37 light-years away.

q: What is the Sun's spectral classification?
explain: The Sun is a G2 V yellow dwarf main-sequence star; the V means it is a main-sequence (dwarf) star.

sources.title: Sun: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Star type : G2 V, yellow dwarf main-sequence star

sources.title: Chapter 1: The Solar System - NASA Science
sources.quote: The Sun is a typical star. Its spectral classification is "G2 V." The G2 part basically means it's a yellow-white star, and the roman numeral V means it's a "main sequence" dwarf star

q: Nuclear fusion in the Sun's core converts hydrogen into which element?
explain: The fusion of hydrogen into helium in the Sun's core, where temperatures top 15 million degrees Celsius, powers the Sun's heat and light.

sources.title: NASA/Marshall Solar Physics
sources.quote: The Sun's core is the central region where nuclear reactions consume hydrogen to form helium. These reactions release the energy that ultimately leaves the surface as visible light.

sources.title: Chapter 1: The Solar System - NASA Science
sources.quote: The Sun's gravity creates extreme pressures and temperatures within its core, sustaining a thermonuclear reaction fusing hydrogen nuclei and producing helium nuclei.

q: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape?
explain: At the event horizon, the velocity needed to escape the black hole exceeds the speed of light, so whatever crosses it cannot get back out.
hook: Events beyond this horizon can never be seen.

sources.title: What Are Black Holes? - NASA
sources.quote: A black hole’s “surface,” called its event horizon, defines the boundary where the velocity needed to escape exceeds the speed of light, which is the speed limit of the cosmos.

sources.title: Black Hole Anatomy - NASA Science
sources.quote: Inside this boundary, the velocity needed to escape the black hole exceeds the speed of light, which is as fast as anything can go. So whatever passes into the event horizon is doomed to stay inside it – even light.

q: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way?
explain: Sagittarius A* is about 27,000 light-years from Earth; the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of it in 2022.

sources.title: Astronomers Reveal First Image of the Black Hole at the Heart of Our Galaxy | Event Horizon Telescope
sources.quote: This is the first image of Sagittarius A* (or Sgr A* for short), the supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxy.

sources.title: Black Hole Image Makes History; NASA Telescopes Coordinated Observations - NASA
sources.quote: also looked at the black hole at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy, called Sagittarius A*, in coordination with EHT.

q: The first-ever image of a black hole, released in 2019, showed the black hole at the center of which galaxy?
explain: The Event Horizon Telescope, a network of eight ground-based radio telescopes, imaged the black hole in elliptical galaxy M87, about 55 million light-years away and 6.5 billion times the Sun's mass.

sources.title: What Are Black Holes? - NASA
sources.quote: In 2019, astronomers using the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) — an international collaboration that networked eight ground-based radio telescopes into a single Earth-size dish — captured an image of a black hole for the first time. It appears as a dark circle silhouetted by an orbiting disk of hot, glowing matter. The supermassive black hole is located at the heart of a galaxy called M87, located about 55 million light-years away

sources.title: Astronomers Reveal First Image of the Black Hole at the Heart of Our Galaxy | Event Horizon Telescope
sources.quote: The breakthrough follows the EHT collaboration’s 2019 release of the first image of a black hole, called M87*, at the centre of the more distant Messier 87 galaxy.

sources.title: Black Hole Image Makes History; NASA Telescopes Coordinated Observations - NASA
sources.quote: The stunning new image shows the shadow of the supermassive black hole in the center of Messier 87 (M87), an elliptical galaxy some 55 million light-years from Earth. This black hole is 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun.

q: What is the nearest large galaxy to our Milky Way?
explain: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is a great spiral galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away and one of the few galaxies visible to the unaided eye.

sources.title: Andromeda Galaxy | Description, Location, Distance, & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: Andromeda Galaxy , (catalog numbers NGC 224 and M31), great spiral galaxy in the constellation Andromeda , the nearest large galaxy. The Andromeda Galaxy is one of the few visible to the unaided eye, appearing as a milky blur. It is located about 2,480,000 light-years from Earth

q: In what year was the Hubble Space Telescope launched?
explain: Hubble launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery on mission STS-31 on April 24, 1990, and was deployed into orbit the next day.

sources.title: STS-31 - NASA
sources.quote: The 35th mission of NASA's Space Shuttle program, Discovery launched on April 24, 1990 to deploy the Hubble Space Telescope.

sources.title: Hubble Space Telescope (HST) | Britannica
sources.quote: The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) was placed into orbit on April 25, 1990, by the crew of the space shuttle Discovery.

q: On what date was the James Webb Space Telescope launched?
explain: Webb launched on an Ariane 5 rocket from Europe's Spaceport in French Guiana and orbits around the second Lagrange point (L2), about 1.5 million km from Earth.

sources.title: Webb's Launch - NASA Science
sources.quote: Webb was launched on on December 25, 2021 on board an Ariane 5 rocket from Ariane Space Spaceport in French Guiana.

sources.title: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) | Britannica
sources.quote: launched by an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou , French Guiana , on December 25, 2021. The JWST has a mirror 6.5 metres (21.3 feet) in diameter, seven times larger than that of the HST, and orbits the Sun in a Lissajous pattern around the second Lagrangian point , about 1.5 million km (930,000 miles) from Earth

q: Which spacecraft became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, in August 2012?
explain: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, crossed the heliopause on Aug. 25, 2012; its twin Voyager 2 reached interstellar space in 2018.

sources.title: Interstellar Mission - NASA Science
sources.quote: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space on Aug. 25, 2012, becoming the first human-made object to do so.

sources.title: NASA Spacecraft Embarks on Historic Journey into Interstellar Space - NASA
sources.quote: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft officially is the first human-made object to venture into interstellar space.

sources.title: Voyager 1 - NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
sources.quote: Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in August 2012 and is the most distant human-made object in existence.

q: What is the name of the gold-plated copper disk of sounds and images from Earth carried by both Voyager spacecraft?
explain: Each Voyager carries a 12-inch gold-plated copper disk with sounds and images selected to portray the story of our world to extraterrestrials.

sources.title: Voyager 1 - NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
sources.quote: Both spacecraft carry a sort of time capsule called the Golden Record, a 12-inch gold-plated copper disk containing sounds and images selected to portray the story of our world to extraterrestrials.

q: In what year did the International Astronomical Union reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet?
explain: At its August 2006 General Assembly, the IAU defined 'planet', leaving eight planets and making Pluto the prototype of the new dwarf planet category.

sources.title: IAU 2006 General Assembly: Result of the IAU Resolution votes
sources.quote: Pluto is a "dwarf planet" by the above definition and is recognized as the prototype of a new category of trans-Neptunian objects.

sources.title: Pluto | Size, Moons, Temperature, & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: In August 2006 the International Astronomical Union (IAU), the organization charged by the scientific community with classifying astronomical objects, voted to remove Pluto from the list of planets and give it the new classification of dwarf planet .

sources.title: About the Planets - NASA Science
sources.quote: Pluto was long considered our solar system's ninth planet. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the International Astronomical Union.

q: Which dwarf planet is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter?
explain: Ceres, discovered in 1801, is the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system and was classified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
hook: Ceres, goddess of grain, gives us the word 'cereal'.

sources.title: Ceres: Facts - NASA Science
sources.quote: Dwarf planet Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and it's the only dwarf planet located in the inner solar system. It was the first member of the asteroid belt to be discovered when Giuseppe Piazzi spotted it in 1801.

sources.title: Ceres | Location, Size, Water, & Facts | Britannica
sources.quote: Ceres , dwarf planet , the largest asteroid in the main asteroid belt, and the first asteroid to be discovered.

q: Under the IAU's 2006 definition, which planet criterion does a dwarf planet fail to meet?
accept: cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit
explain: Both planets and dwarf planets orbit the Sun and are massive enough to be nearly round, but a dwarf planet has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit and is not a satellite.

sources.title: IAU 2006 General Assembly: Result of the IAU Resolution votes
sources.quote: A "dwarf planet" is a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a hydrostatic equilibrium (nearly round) shape [2], (c) has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit, and (d) is not a satellite.

sources.title: Why Is Pluto No Longer a Planet? | Britannica
sources.quote: Pluto is now classified as a dwarf planet because, while it is large enough to have become spherical, it is not big enough to exert its orbital dominance and clear the neighborhood surrounding its orbit.
